text:
Some people can feel their body just fine, but the moment a real feeling starts coming up in a session, they slide away from it, maybe by explaining it or by agreeing with whatever the therapist says. If that's you, look for a therapist who catches you sliding away and helps you stay with the feeling. A few talk therapies are built to do just that.

In Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy, the therapist points out each slide as it happens and helps you turn back toward the feeling, watching your body for signs of anxiety as you go. Most people who come to this therapy get overwhelmed easily, so they usually get a slower version of it, where the therapist helps them settle whenever the anxiety climbs too high. Then there's Affect Phobia Therapy, for when one feeling in particular scares you, grief for example: it gets you used to that feeling bit by bit, at a pace your anxiety can handle.

And some people's trouble is with being treated kindly: when someone cares about them, they can't let it in. For them, Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy first makes sure they don't feel alone with what comes up, then follows how it feels in the body.

As with water therapy, I'd ask before booking: "What do you do when I start moving away from a feeling, and what if I get overwhelmed?" If the answer leaves no room for you to slow down, or to disagree with them about what you're feeling, keep looking.

text:
Maybe pain is what brought you to this guide. If yours has lasted months, and a doctor has checked and found no injury or disease to explain it, two therapies are worth knowing about.

In Pain Reprocessing Therapy, you learn that the pain is a false alarm, your brain signaling danger where there isn't any, partly by paying close attention to how it feels in your body. Then, a little at a time, you go back to things you've been avoiding because of it, like going for walks.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain. There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.

The second therapy is for pain that seems bound up with stress and feelings about the people in your life. Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy works on those feelings directly. Much of the therapy is letting out anger and other feelings you've held back, and rehearsing in role-play what you'd say to someone you've never stood up to.

In a 2024 trial of veterans aged 60 and up, this therapy beat CBT: 63% had their pain drop by at least 30% afterward, compared to 17% with CBT. That's a lower bar than 0 or 1 out of 10, so the two trials' numbers can't be compared.

I haven't found a trial comparing the two. So if your pain seems tied to stress or to people in your life, I'd start with the second, and otherwise with the first. I'd also ask a therapist where they trained in that therapy, and keep track of how it's going the way I describe in the last section, How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping.

text:
If you can feel your body just fine by now but you still slip away the moment a feeling comes up in a session (you start explaining it, or agree with whatever the therapist says just to get past it), there's Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy. The ISTDP therapist catches you each time they notice you slipping, and asks what you're feeling right then.

It's usually anxiety about the feeling that makes you slip away, so the therapist also watches for its signs, like tense muscles, sighing, or your thinking going foggy, to tell when it's getting to be too much for you. If you can only take a little of that anxiety, like most people who try this therapy, you'd get a slower version of it, where the therapist stops to help you settle whenever the anxiety climbs.

If it's one feeling in particular that scares you, like grief, Affect Phobia Therapy treats that fear a lot like a phobia, getting you used to the feeling bit by bit, at a pace your anxiety can handle.

The therapist works to keep you from feeling alone with whatever comes up, and when some of their care does get in, they ask what that's like and where you feel it in your body.

All three keep steering you back toward your feelings, which can get to be too intense sometimes. So before booking, I'd ask the kind of thing I'd ask a water therapist: "What happens if I get overwhelmed, or if you say I'm dodging a feeling and I don't think I am?"
